name: Tribulus terrestris

card.summary: Herbal 'testosterone booster' sold since the 1980s; controlled studies have not consistently shown a hormone effect.
card.note: NCCIH says safety not proven; athlete bodies discourage use.

quick.overview:
Tribulus is a spiny plant whose extracts are sold as testosterone and libido supplements.

Controlled human studies have not consistently shown a testosterone effect, and no high-quality trial supports strength gains.
quick.mechanism: Marketing points to steroidal saponins such as protodioscin; supporting evidence is mainly from rodent and primate studies.
quick.risks: Safety in humans has not been proven according to the NCCIH. Sheep suffer photodermatitis from the plant; confirmed human reactions are not documented.

lead: Tribulus terrestris (puncture vine, goathead, Gokshura) is a spiny, low-growing annual of the caltrop family, native to warm regions of Eurasia and Africa and widely naturalised elsewhere [1][2]. Its fruit, leaf and root extracts come from Chinese and Ayurvedic herbal traditions and, since the 1980s, have been sold as dietary supplements aimed at raising testosterone for muscle building and at supporting libido and sexual function [1][3].

In looksmaxxing and bodybuilding circles it is usually taken for its appearance-related promise: the idea that higher androgen signalling could support muscle fullness, leanness and drive, which in turn feed into physique. It is typically sold as a standardised extract (often labelled by saponin percentage) and stacked with other over-the-counter 'test boosters' such as D-aspartic acid, zinc or tongkat ali [4][5].

Research on the plant includes rat and primate experiments on sexual behaviour and hormones, small controlled trials in resistance-trained men and CrossFit athletes, and trials of multi-ingredient products in women with sexual-desire complaints, men with fertility problems and people with diabetes or PCOS [6][7][8][9][10][11][12]. Wikipedia reports that controlled studies have not consistently shown an effect on testosterone levels, and that the US National Center for Complementary and Integrative Health says safety has not been proven [1].

chain: Extract sold for steroidal saponins such as protodioscin

angle.text: People take Tribulus because proponents say it raises or supports testosterone, which governs muscle mass, body-fat distribution and drive. The hoped-for payoff is a fuller, leaner physique from training. Published trials of the plain extract in trained men have mostly measured strength and body composition rather than hormones [6][7].

paras: Linnaeus described the species in 1753 from Mediterranean specimens [2]. It is a taprooted plant whose stems radiate flat along the ground, with small yellow five-petalled flowers and a fruit that splits into hard, spined burs. The burs resemble goat or bull heads, which gives rise to names such as goathead, and they are sharp enough to puncture bicycle tyres and bare feet [1]. The genus name comes from the Latin word for the caltrop, an ancient spiked anti-personnel device, itself derived from a Greek word for the water chestnut [1][2].

Grokipedia describes traditional uses across Asia, Europe and Africa as a diuretic, tonic, aphrodisiac and remedy for urinary complaints, with the Ayurvedic name Gokshura referring to a cow's hoof and the Chinese name Bai ji li to a white-spined caltrop [2]. Leaves and shoots are eaten in East Asia, and the stems have been used as a thickener [1]. The plant is also known as an invasive weed and is a 'declared plant' in South Australia, where transport and sale are prohibited [1].

Extracts, usually standardised for steroidal saponins such as protodioscin, are marketed as testosterone boosters and libido aids, and also appear in multi-ingredient 'HGH complex' and men's-health formulas [1][3][13]. Forum users on T Nation describe it in several ways: as a staple of daily supplement stacks alongside creatine and protein, as something taken before bed on the theory that it supports overnight hormone production, and as a libido aid taken with D-aspartic acid, ashwagandha and zinc [14][15][16].

Some users report taking it after anabolic-steroid or prohormone use in the hope of supporting natural hormone recovery, a practice described in forum posts; one user said it was the only supplement out of many that seemed to do anything for them, while another asked what to watch for when using it alongside a urologist's care [17][18]. One poster says it works for them through lowering SHBG, the protein that binds testosterone in blood [19]. These are individual anecdotes.

The saponin protodioscin is the compound most often cited as the active principle. In castrated and intact rats, a protodioscin-containing extract changed sexual behaviour and intracavernous pressure, with authors proposing an androgen-related mechanism [4]. A study in primates, rabbits and rats examined hormonal effects in relation to erectile function [5]. A review of the plant's pharmacology summarises reported antioxidant, anti-inflammatory, antidiabetic and urological actions, mostly from laboratory work [3]. These findings come from animals and cell models; extrapolation to human testosterone is what the clinical trials below address.

Wikipedia notes the plant causes photodermatitis in sheep (geeldikkop or tribulosis), attributed to compounds that accumulate after chlorophyll breakdown, and that harmful effects in people have not been confirmed; a claim of liver damage at high doses carries a citation-needed flag [1]. Grokipedia mentions harmane-type alkaloids linked to limb weakness in sheep that graze it [2]. Supplements are not pre-approved by the FDA in the US, and the NCCIH states that safety has not been proven [1]. The Australian Institute of Sport discourages athlete use of Tribulus supplements, citing a lack of good evidence of effectiveness or safety [1].

In an 8-week study of 15 resistance-trained men randomised to tribulus or placebo during periodised resistance training, neither group changed in body weight, fat percentage, dietary intake or mood, and the authors concluded the supplement did not enhance body composition or performance [6].

A 6-week single-blind trial in 30 trained male CrossFit athletes gave 770 mg per day or placebo and tracked muscle-damage enzymes, inflammation markers and antioxidant status; the groups differed in lactate dehydrogenase, C-reactive protein and total antioxidant status at the end, while the authors noted no significant decrease in muscle-damage or inflammation markers in the treated group [7]. A 2025 registered study examined acute effects on anaerobic power and sprint performance in combat-sport athletes [20].

A randomised comparison in 70 older men with reduced libido gave a combination product containing Tribulus, an alga extract and glucosamine versus daily tadalafil for two months, measuring testosterone, nocturnal erections and questionnaires [8]. A 60-man placebo-controlled trial of a myo-inositol, Tribulus, alga and Biovis product for 90 days reported improvements in sperm concentration and motility and in DNA fragmentation [10]. In both, Tribulus was one of several ingredients, so effects cannot be attributed to it alone.

Other human work includes a pragmatic trial in overweight women with PCOS in which a herbal combination including a Tribulus tablet, added to lifestyle support, was compared with lifestyle alone and reduced oligomenorrhoea [9]; a placebo-controlled trial in 98 women with type 2 diabetes in which a 1000 mg daily extract lowered blood glucose and cholesterol over three months [11]; and registered trials in women with low sexual desire and in men with oligospermia [12][21][22][23]. A 2024 Annals of Internal Medicine evidence map found two low-quality trials of the plant for menopausal sexual symptoms, too varied for firm conclusions, and Wikipedia reports that no high-quality randomised trial has shown strength or anabolic effects [1].

lore.intro: Tribulus is discussed on T Nation and similar forums as a classic over-the-counter 'test booster' used in supplement stacks and post-cycle routines, with opinions ranging from enthusiastic to indifferent [14][17].

claims.claim: Tribulus raises testosterone and supports muscle building
claims.believers: Users stack it with creatine and protein and report taking it daily, and some say the effect on libido and training drive is noticeable [15][16].
claims.experts: Controlled studies have not consistently shown a testosterone effect in humans, and an 8-week trial in resistance-trained men found no change in body composition [1][6].

claims.claim: Taking it before bed matches the body's overnight hormone peak
claims.believers: A forum thread proposes taking test boosters at night so they coincide with peak hormone production [16].
claims.experts: No published human studies have tested bedtime timing of Tribulus.

claims.claim: It boosts libido and sexual function
claims.believers: Users with low drive describe adding it to stacks with D-aspartic acid and ashwagandha [18][19].
claims.experts: Rat studies reported effects on sexual behaviour [4]; human trials are mainly of multi-ingredient products or in women, and an evidence map found only two low-quality trials for menopausal symptoms [1][8].

claims.claim: It helps hormone recovery after steroid or prohormone use
claims.believers: Some forum posters describe using it in place of or alongside post-cycle therapy [17].
claims.experts: No published trials have examined Tribulus for recovery after anabolic-steroid use.

claims.believers: One user says Tribulus 'reduces SHBG' and works for them for that reason [19].
claims.experts: The hormonal rodent and primate work examined androgen-related effects [5]; no published human trial in the sources reports an SHBG mechanism.
